bib.title: Present Imperatives and Future Outlook (Chapter 17, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed.)

question: What technology, privacy, security, legal and cultural trends will shape data warehousing over the next 10 to 20 years?
contributions: Surveys expected technology advances, privacy and security pressures, intellectual-property limits and cultural trends for data warehousing, as of 2002.

results.claim: Worked storage estimate for personal data-collecting transducers: one 40-byte record per person per second for 300 million people needs 378,432 TB per year.
results.setup: 300 million US people, one record per second, 24x365, 40-byte text and numeric records, no images or maps
results.quote: records thus generated are 40 bytes wide, this would require 378,432 TB

limits: Written in 2002; technology predictions (Internet appliance, DoCoMo, DSL, NT, SANs, ASPs) are dated.
Post-9/11 security framing; opinion, no empirical data.
Privacy architecture list predates GDPR/CCPA; HIPAA and COPPA described as not fully implemented in 2002.
Authors concede the privacy list is a speculative scenario for advance planning.
practices: Treat ingest as part of publishing the right data: warehouse is the platform for cleaned data and sophisticated clients (data mining) should not do their own primary extraction (p.384).
Fix incompatible or lost data at the source: integration and data quality cannot be cleaned downstream, so the warehouse manager should sit on the EAI architecture board (p.386).
Application packages (including ERP) should provide flexible, high-performance extraction of all their data into a separate warehouse; packages cannot be the warehouse (p.386).
Hand off observation sets as files to data mining tools and take results back, using drill-across of conformed dimensions (p.384-385).
Consolidate personal information into one cleaned database with two security sensitivity levels, an audit database of uses, subject access/correction interfaces, and true expunging (p.378-379).
Isolate the database server behind a packet-filtering gateway accepting only trusted application servers (p.382).
Use a central LDAP server for role-based authentication of all outside access (p.382).
Distribute the warehouse across machines, OSs, locations and copies; keep parallel communication paths, extended SANs and daily offline backups, checking media readability years ahead (p.380-382).
Be careful about collecting data from outside sources because of copyright and licence exposure; fair use is weak for enterprises (p.383).
Prefer an ASP-like entity running an in-house warehouse with skills sharing over a pure remote ASP; write the level-of-service agreement yourself (p.387).
Close by listening to the business: the job is to publish the right data (p.387).
